title: Personal Project Criterion C: Reflecting With…
summary: Personal Project criterion C explained for MYP Year 5 students, with reflection examples, product evaluation tips, and a clear guide to using evidence well.
body_markdown:
Personal Project criterion C asks you to do two things: **explain the impact of the project on yourself or your learning, and evaluate your product against your success criteria** . For an MYP Year 5 student, that means showing what changed because of the project and judging what your finished work actually achieved.


Finishing the product can feel like crossing the finish line. Then you open the report and discover another task: making sense of everything that happened.


To follow that process, imagine Maya, a hypothetical student who created a beginner’s recipe booklet. Her learning goal was to understand how to adapt recipes for inexperienced cooks. Her product is finished, but her reflection begins with a question: what does the evidence allow her to claim?


### Personal Project criterion C: the requirements


The current three-criterion framework identifies Criterion C as **Reflecting** , worth a maximum of **8 achievement levels** . Its requirements, reproduced in school guides for 2025-2026, distinguish two strands:


Strand What you need to demonstrate


C.i Explain the impact of the project on yourself or your learning.


C.ii Evaluate the product based on the success criteria.


At the **7-8 band** , the descriptor requires an explanation of impact and a product evaluation fully supported with specific evidence or detailed examples. Check the rubric supplied by your supervisor before submitting, especially if an online resource uses an older four-criterion framework.


RevisionDojo’s[MYP Personal Project criteria guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-personal-project-criteria) explains how this fits alongside Planning and Applying skills.


Before drafting, gather:


- Your original learning goal and product success criteria.
- Evidence of your starting point and later understanding.
- Product tests, photographs, feedback, or other relevant results.
- Specific strengths, limitations, and reasons for your judgments.


### Explain what changed in your learning


Maya’s first attempt reads: “I learned cooking skills and became more confident.”


That identifies an impact, but the reader cannot yet understand its significance. What could she do afterward that she could not do before? What experience caused that change?


Her revised explanation might say:


> “At the beginning, I assumed that a beginner would understand instructions such as ‘simmer until reduced.’ During my first recipe test, a participant asked what both terms meant. I learned that knowing a technique and explaining it are different skills. I began replacing technical instructions with observable signs, such as changes in texture. This changed how I judge whether my explanations are clear.”


This works because it connects a starting assumption, a specific experience, and a change in understanding. It also explains why the experience mattered.


A useful drafting sequence is **before, experience, change, significance** . Treat it as a thinking aid rather than a compulsory IB structure.


Your impact could involve subject knowledge, independence, approaches to learning (ATL) skills, or a changed perspective. Choose the changes you can explain convincingly. A catalogue of every learner profile attribute usually leaves little room for depth.


### Keep Criterion B and Criterion C distinct


Criterion B explains how you applied ATL skills to achieve your learning goal and product. Criterion C considers the impact of the experience.


Maya might discuss using communication skills in both sections. In B, she explains how she designed and used feedback questions. In C, she explains how the responses changed her understanding of an audience’s needs.


The same event can support different analysis. Repeating the same paragraph adds little.


### Evaluate the product against your success criteria


Maya now returns to the success criteria established during planning. She resists the temptation to replace a difficult target with something her booklet already does well.


Evaluation means weighing strengths and limitations. For each criterion, connect **the standard, the evidence, and your judgment** .


The following results are illustrative, not real student data:


Original success criterion Hypothetical evidence Supported judgment


Include six recipes with numbered instructions. The final booklet contains six recipes, each with numbered steps. Met: the required content and structure are present.


Each recipe takes no more than 30 minutes for a beginner. Two beginner testers take 38 and 41 minutes to complete one recipe. Not met for that recipe: its preparation time was underestimated.


At least four of five testers rate the instructions clear. Four select “clear”; one identifies an unexplained cooking term. Met within this small test group, with a remaining clarity limitation.


The judgment should follow from the evidence. A photograph can establish that a booklet exists, but it cannot demonstrate that beginners understand it. Match the evidence to the claim.


A student asks for honest feedback while a tiny inspector suggests a boat for a toy car beside a sagging bridge.


### Explain the limits of your evidence


Maya’s five testers provide useful feedback, but their responses cannot establish that every beginner will understand her booklet. Their cooking experience may also differ.


She can acknowledge this briefly: “The responses suggest the instructions were clear for most participants in this test, although a larger group with varied cooking experience would provide stronger evidence.”


That qualification makes her conclusion more precise. Specific evidence helps the reader assess both the achievement and the uncertainty.


### Turn a weakness into a useful conclusion


An unmet criterion deserves analysis rather than an excuse.


Maya could write:


> “The timing criterion was not achieved for the pasta recipe. Both beginner testers exceeded 30 minutes because chopping and measuring took longer than in my own trial. I had based the estimate on my familiarity with the recipe. A revised version would give separate preparation and cooking times, tested with beginners.”


The improvement follows directly from the limitation. Suggestions such as “manage my time better” would not address the problem identified here.


Reviewing RevisionDojo’s[Personal Project exemplars](https://www.revisiondojo.com/coursework-exemplars/subject/myp-personal-project) can help you examine how evidence and analysis connect. Preserve your own wording, experiences, and judgments.


### Review your reflection before submission


Read your draft once for each strand. First, check whether you explain meaningful changes in yourself or your learning. Then check whether you evaluate the product against every success criterion, with evidence supporting your conclusions.


Watch for unsupported praise, lists of activities, and feedback quoted without interpretation. RevisionDojo’s guide to[common Personal Project mistakes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/common-myp-personal-project-mistakes-e0513f75) offers another useful review point.


Maya finishes with a booklet that has strengths and limitations, and a clearer understanding of how beginners learn. Her report makes both visible.


RevisionDojo brings the wider process together through its[MYP Personal Project student guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-personal-project-ultimate-guide) , Coursework Library examples, and[Personal Project Grader](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grader/rubric/personal-project) . Use these resources to review your own draft, then discuss uncertainties with your supervisor. The final reflection should remain your explanation of what the project taught you and what your evidence shows.
